caption: Centrifugal pump seen along the shaft. title: The power plant and energy
goals: Follow energy from fuel to the socket and name each conversion.

q: Guess: a combined-cycle plant burns fuel worth 1000 MW of heat and sends out 580 MW of electricity. Where did the other 420 MW go?

text: It was destroyed in the turbines.
why: Energy can't be destroyed. It was converted to something less useful.

text: It left as heat, mostly in the stack gas and the cooling water.
why: Right. Conservation of energy: every MW in comes out somewhere, and most of the loss is low-temperature heat.

text: It is stored in the steam.
why: The steam circulates in a closed loop; over time it can't store energy indefinitely.

p: A power plant does not make energy. It converts one form into another that people can use: electricity. Energy is the ability to do work, and the
(Mayer 1842, Joule 1843) says it can be neither created nor destroyed, only converted. Every megawatt that leaves on the grid came in as fuel. What doesn't become electricity leaves as heat.
Different plants differ only in how they get to
, because every large plant ends with a generator:

h: The steam cycle in one loop

p: In a steam plant, very pure (demineralised) water is pumped into a boiler, turned into high-pressure superheated steam, expanded through a steam turbine that drives a generator, condensed back into water in a condenser, and pumped back. The same water goes round and round. The deck's example plant runs at
and
; Rumaila's HP steam is similar at about
and
Water must be free of salts and gases (O₂, CO₂) because it circulates forever. Anything dissolved in it concentrates in the boiler and attacks the metal. Module 11 covers this.

Efficiency = useful output ÷ energy input. Because energy is conserved, the rest is not "lost" in the sense of disappearing: it leaves as heat, mostly up the stack and into the cooling water. A gas turbine alone converts roughly 40% of its fuel to electricity. Adding an HRSG and steam turbine to use its hot exhaust lifts that to about 58–61%: Siemens set records of
(2011) with combined-cycle plants.
Rumaila is a combined-cycle plant: gas turbines, each followed by an HRSG, with the HRSGs feeding steam to the steam turbine. That is the subject of Module 10.

case: Why does adding an HRSG and a steam turbine behind a gas turbine raise plant efficiency so much?
steps: Look at the gas turbine's loss
Its exhaust leaves at about 600 °C. The deck calls this "the biggest disadvantage of every gas turbine".
600 °C gas is hot enough to make high-pressure steam, the same kind a whole coal plant uses.
The HRSG turns that exhaust heat into steam; the steam turbine turns the steam into more rotation and more electricity. The gas now leaves the stack at about 100 °C.
Same fuel, extra output, so efficiency rises from about 40% to about 60%.

q: Guess: a section of cooling water pipe is isolated full of water by two closed valves and then warms up in the sun. What happens?

why: Water expands only a little, but it can't be compressed, so even a small expansion drives pressure up very fast.

text: Pressure rises sharply and the pipe can leak or burst unless there is a relief valve.
why: Right. That is why isolatable liquid-full sections get relief valves.
Rising pressure prevents boiling; the risk is overpressure.

p: measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules: how fast they move. Units: kelvin (K), degree Celsius (°C), Fahrenheit (°F). A change of 1 K equals a change of 1 °C; 0 K = −273.15 °C.

In a flowing liquid, total energy per volume stays constant along the pipe (ignoring friction):
p + ½ρc² + ρgh = constant
where p is static pressure, ½ρc² dynamic pressure (ρ density, c velocity) and ρgh the pressure from height. Where the pipe narrows, velocity rises and static pressure falls. This is how an

h: Thermal expansion: the most common source of damage

p: Almost everything expands when heated. What happens next depends on whether it can move:

(practically incompressible): pressure rises extremely fast because the liquid can't squeeze. A closed, full water pipe that warms up will start leaking at flanges and joints or burst. So closed water systems get

A bigger leak is louder. Superheated steam and compressed air leaks are louder than wet steam leaks. Silencers are fitted where noise is expected: air intakes, the gas outlet, safety valves, start-up vents and blow-off lines.

What you see as "steam" is condensed droplets, which form only once the steam has cooled below its boiling point, some distance from the leak. Right at a superheated leak the jet is clear and extremely dangerous.

steps: About 1 mm per metre per 100 K. So 30 m × 5.2 ≈ 156 mm.

Carbon steel corrodes fast in acidic water and much more slowly in mildly alkaline water. The deck's chart shows relative corrosion against pH at 25 °C: high at low pH, lowest and nearly flat in the alkaline range (roughly pH 10 to 12 at 25 °C), rising again in strongly alkaline water. Power plant water is kept just alkaline, in that low-corrosion window.
Steel in hot, clean, alkaline, oxygen-poor water grows a thin, tight black layer of
that protects the metal underneath. Other iron oxides matter too:
, red, forms with oxygen (rust);
, black, is stable only above about 570 °C (the deck says 560 °C in one place and 570 °C in its figure), in the hottest superheater tubes. Good chemistry keeps the magnetite layer intact.

ul: alkalising only with volatile chemicals (ammonia) that travel with the steam and leave no solids behind. Phosphate, by contrast, is a solid that stays in the drum water.

fast-flowing water, especially at bends and where water and steam mix, dissolves the magnetite layer faster than it can re-form, and the pipe wall thins. Worst at around 150 °C in carbon steel. A classic cause of feedwater and economizer pipe failures.
